transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, um, I guess I’m here because of what’s been going on at work. I’m in transportation, I drive, and... well, it’s dispatch. Dispatch and the compliance department. They’ve been tracking my route changes through the computer system, and I mean, I know we have GPS and all that, but this is different. They are specifically zeroing in on every single turn I make, every little deviation from the manifest, and logging it in real-time. 

And it’s not just the computer system, either. It’s the radio, too. I’ll be driving, just trying to do my job and keep to the schedule, and I hear these little comments on the radio from dispatch—just these subtle things, little phrases that you might miss if you weren't paying attention, but I know they're about me and where I am on my route. 

And, you know, I’ve tried to say something about it, and people just brush it off. They tell me it’s just normal oversight, that everybody gets monitored for safety and efficiency or whatever corporate excuse they want to use, but I know that’s not true. It's not just standard procedure. I can tell. I can tell that certain drivers, the ones on the same shift as me, are actually reporting on me. They’re watching what I do and feeding it back to compliance, and it’s just... it’s every single shift now, and I just can't get anyone at the depot to admit what's actually happening.

Before all of this started happening at work, have you ever had similar experiences in the past—times when you felt like people were watching you or coordinating against you, even in different settings or jobs?

Well, um, no. No, honestly, I haven't. I mean, I've worked other jobs before this one, obviously. Right after I got my associate's degree, I worked at a logistics warehouse doing inventory control, and then I drove a delivery van for a local florist for a couple of years before I got my current licensing and moved into this kind of transport. And back then... I mean, sure, bosses can be annoying, right? They might check your timesheets or ask why a delivery took ten minutes longer than expected because of traffic, but it was never, ever like this. 

I never felt this... this heavy, constant scrutiny. Like, at the florist, my manager was a bit of a micromanager about the temperature in the back of the van so the lilies wouldn't wilt, but she wasn't *tracking* me, you know? She wasn't having the other drivers whisper about my routes on the radio or coordinating with some corporate compliance office to log my every move. I’ve always been a good worker. I’ve always just kept my head down, done my routes, and gone home. 

I don't know why they picked me now, at this specific company. It's just this depot. It's like a switch flipped recently. Before I started dealing with this specific dispatch team, everything in my life was totally normal, completely fine. I never had to look over my shoulder or wonder if the static on the dispatch channel was actually them calling out my truck number to the other drivers on the road. So, no, I've never dealt with anything even close to this before. It's just them. It's just what's happening right now.

When your coworkers or supervisors tell you that this is just standard monitoring and there's nothing unusual happening, do you think there's any possibility they could be right, or are you completely certain that what you're experiencing is real and deliberate targeting?

No, no, there is absolutely zero possibility that they are right. Zero. I mean, when they sit there in the depot office and try to tell me, 'Oh, it’s just normal oversight, everyone gets monitored,' I just... I know they're lying to my face. Like I was saying, I'm here because dispatch and compliance have been tracking my route changes through the computer system, and it is *not* the normal GPS tracking. Standard monitoring is checking your mileage at the end of the week, or maybe seeing if a truck idled too long at a rest stop. It is *not* what they are doing to me. 

And the radio... standard monitoring doesn't explain the little comments on the radio. I’ll be driving, say I have to take a slight detour because of construction on the interstate, and the exact second I hit my blinker, I hear the radio crackle. And dispatch will say some little phrase, something disguised as a traffic update or a joke, but it's exactly about where I just turned. How is that standard? It's not. 

And even when people, like my supervisor or the HR rep, say it’s just normal oversight and try to make me feel like I'm making a big deal out of nothing, I can tell certain drivers are reporting on me. I can literally see it happening. I'll see one of the guys from the morning shift lingering near my loading bay, watching me check my manifest, and then ten minutes later, compliance is suddenly pinging my dashboard terminal with a route audit. They are coordinating it. I am completely, one hundred percent certain that this is deliberate targeting. I mean, if it were just standard procedure, why would they hide it in the radio chatter? Why would they use the other drivers to feed information back to compliance instead of just talking to me directly? It just... it doesn't make any sense to call it normal when it's so obviously designed to watch my every single move.

When you think about dispatch and compliance tracking you through the radio and having other drivers report on you—do you believe they're using some kind of special technology or surveillance method that wouldn't normally be possible, or do you think they're just using the regular GPS and radio systems in an unusually coordinated way?

Well, I mean, it's... it's a mix, I think. I don't think they've got, like, microchips in my brain or anything out of a sci-fi movie, if that's what you mean. It's the regular equipment, but it's *how* they're using it. Like I said, I’m here because dispatch and compliance have been tracking my route changes through the computer system, right? The dashboard terminals, the GPS... that's all standard issue in the cabs. But they've got it rigged or programmed or... or something, to isolate my feed. 

And the radios, it's the standard dispatch frequency, but they know exactly when to key the mic. They know exactly when I'm listening. It's the coordination that's so unbelievable. I'll hear those little comments on the radio—just a quick remark about a "detour" or "watching your speed on the curve"—and it's timed perfectly to the second I'm making that exact maneuver. You can't do that with just casual observation. Someone has to be staring at a screen, specifically my screen, and relaying it to the person on the mic. 

And then there's the other drivers. That's the part that really gets me. It's not just the technology; it's the human element. Because even when people say it’s just normal oversight, you know, the HR people sitting in their nice quiet offices, I can tell certain drivers are reporting on me. I see them. I see the way they look at my truck in the yard. I'll be doing my pre-trip inspection, checking the air brakes, kicking the tires, and there's always one of them—usually Gary from the overnight shift, or sometimes that new guy, Mark—just lingering. Holding a clipboard but not writing anything down. Just watching me. And then they get on their radios, or they pull out their phones, and suddenly my terminal pings with a "random" compliance check. 

So, no, it's not alien technology, but it's definitely not just normal use of the systems. It's a massive, coordinated effort. They are using everything they have—the GPS, the dispatch radio, the other drivers—all tied together to keep this constant, suffocating watch on me. And I just... I can't figure out why it's just me. Why are they wasting all these resources, all this time, just to track a mid-level transport driver? It takes so much effort to coordinate the radio chatter with the dashboard tracking, and then to have the other drivers physically watching me at the depot... it's exhausting just thinking about the logistics of it. But they're doing it. I know they're doing it.

When you think about how dispatch and compliance are coordinating all of this—the GPS tracking, the radio timing, the other drivers watching you—do you think what they're doing is something that's physically possible for them to do with the equipment and people they have, or does it seem like it would require something that shouldn't be possible?

Well, see, that's exactly what I spend half my nights trying to figure out, because it *is* physically possible. It doesn't require magic or anything supernatural, it just requires an unbelievable amount of dedication to ruining my life. I mean, like I keep trying to explain to everyone, the entire reason I’m even here talking to you is because dispatch and compliance have been tracking my route changes through the computer system and making those little comments on the radio. They have the exact equipment they need to do it right there in the office! 

If you walk past the main dispatch center at the depot, they have this massive wall of monitors. I've seen it through the blinds when I go to grab my morning manifest. They have the entire GPS grid up, all the truck numbers blinking in real-time. So all it takes is for one compliance officer to sit there, isolate my truck's feed on their screen, and just watch my dot move across the map. And the radio microphone is sitting right there on the desk next to the keyboard. When I take a turn, they just press the button and broadcast their little coded messages to the rest of the fleet. It's literally just a click of a mouse and a push of a button for them.

And as for the people involved... well, again, even when people in management say it’s just normal oversight, I can tell certain drivers are reporting on me. It doesn't take some impossible sci-fi gadget for Gary or Mark to stand by the loading dock with a cell phone and text the compliance office that I'm checking my air brakes or looking at my paperwork. They have eyes, they have phones, they have the company radios. The ELD in my cab—the electronic logging device—it already tracks engine idle time, hard braking, route deviations. It's meant for Department of Transportation safety regulations, supposedly, but it's a two-way data stream. They just hijacked the purpose of it for me. 

So, yes, it is entirely physically possible with the exact equipment we use every single day. What's impossible to understand is *why*. Why are they wasting all these company resources? Do you know how much they pay the compliance guys per hour? To have them, and the dispatchers, and the other drivers all hyper-focused on my routes... the payroll alone for this kind of surveillance must be astronomical. It's a logistical nightmare to coordinate all those moving parts just to watch one woman drive a transport truck. But they are doing it. They absolutely are, and they're using the standard depot equipment to pull it off, just... weaponizing it against me.

You've explained that they're using the GPS monitors, the radio system, and having other drivers watch you—all equipment and people that actually exist at your depot. If someone wanted to do exactly what you're describing, is there anything about what they're doing that would be impossible according to the laws of nature, or is it just something that would be very difficult and unlikely for them to actually do?

No, it doesn't break the laws of physics. There's no magic involved, no bending of reality or anything like that. It's just... it's incredibly, incredibly difficult and tedious. But that's exactly why it's so maddening when people don't believe me! Because it is entirely possible in the real world. 

Like I keep saying, and I know I probably sound like a broken record to you by now, but I’m here because dispatch and compliance have been tracking my route changes through the computer system and making those little comments on the radio. None of that requires breaking the laws of nature! The computers are right there on their desks, the radios transmit on standard frequencies. It's just basic technology. And even when people try to gaslight me and say it’s just normal oversight, like they're just checking my mileage or making sure I'm not idling too long, I can tell certain drivers are reporting on me. I see them doing it with my own two eyes. Gary doesn't need supernatural powers to stand by a loading dock and send a text message to compliance. It's just a guy in a high-vis vest with a smartphone. 

So, no, it's not impossible at all. It's just... it's highly unlikely that a logistics company would waste this much payroll and effort on one transport driver. That's the part that makes it feel so crazy, even to me. The sheer amount of coordination it takes—to have the drivers physically watching me in the yard, and then compliance monitoring my exact dot on the computer screen, and then dispatch timing the radio comments perfectly to my turns—it's a logistical nightmare. The man-hours alone! It's so much effort just to watch me. But they are doing it. They absolutely are. And I just don't understand why they can't just let me drive my routes in peace instead of turning the entire depot into this massive, exhausting surveillance operation. It's like I can't even take a breath in my own cab without someone logging it into a spreadsheet somewhere, and it just... it doesn't make sense why they'd go through all this trouble, but they are.

Have you tried to gather concrete evidence of this surveillance—like recording the radio conversations, documenting the times you hear those comments, or keeping a log of when you see Gary or Mark watching you?

Well, I have tried, yes, but you have to understand how incredibly difficult it is to play detective when you're behind the wheel of a commercial vehicle. I tried using the voice memo app on my phone to catch the radio chatter, but the background noise in the cab—the diesel engine, the road vibration, the air brakes—it completely drowns out the nuance of what they're saying on the recording. And I can't exactly hold my phone up to the speaker while I'm navigating a 53-foot trailer through a tight interchange, right? By the time I hear one of those little comments on the radio, the ones perfectly timed to my route changes, the moment is already gone. 

And I did start keeping a log! I bought this little blue spiral notebook specifically for it, kept it tucked right in my glovebox. I'd write down the date, the time, the exact location in the yard every single time I saw Gary lingering by the loading dock, or when Mark would pull out his phone right as I was doing my pre-trip inspection. But the problem is, who do I even show it to? I know I keep repeating myself, but it's the entire reason I’m here talking to you—I’m here because dispatch and compliance have been tracking my route changes through the computer system and making those little comments on the radio, and even when people in management try to brush it off and say it’s just normal oversight, I can tell certain drivers are reporting on me. 

I actually tried to bring it up to the safety manager last week. I didn't show him the whole notebook, I just mentioned the pattern of people lingering around my truck, and he gave me this whole condescending speech about how everyone is just doing their jobs and it's just 'normal oversight' for a busy depot. He told me Gary was probably just waiting for his bay to clear. But it's not normal! It's not normal for Gary to stand in the freezing rain for twenty minutes just watching me check my tire pressure without writing a single thing on his clipboard. You can feel it when someone is watching you with a purpose, you know? It’s not a casual glance. They’re taking inventory of my actions to feed back to the office. 

So now I feel like I have to hide the notebook. Because if they know I'm actively gathering evidence of them reporting on me, who knows what they'll do with the computer system next. Maybe they'll wipe my ELD data or say I falsified my logs. It's just a constant, exhausting battle trying to document it all while still trying to do my actual job safely, and I'm just running out of energy to keep up with it all.

If you were to step back for a moment—is it possible that some of those radio comments or those times you see Gary watching you could just be coincidences, or are you completely certain that every single instance is definitely part of the coordinated surveillance against you?

Coincidence? I mean... look, I get why you'd ask that. If you weren't there, if you didn't live it every single day, it probably sounds like maybe I'm just reading too much into things. And if it happened just once or twice, sure. If I take a detour because of a wreck on the interstate and suddenly the radio cracks with some weird, vague comment about 'taking the long way around,' maybe that's just a joke. Maybe Gary just happens to be standing in the freezing rain by bay four once in a blue moon because he locked himself out of the breakroom. 

But you have to look at the whole picture, the sheer volume of it. It’s not just one isolated thing, it's every single shift. I know I keep bringing this back to the exact same point, and I know I've said it a dozen times today already, but it really is the entire reason I’m even here talking to you right now—I’m here because dispatch and compliance have been tracking my route changes through the computer system and making those little comments on the radio. It's a constant, everyday thing. And even when people in the office try to brush me off and say it’s just normal oversight, like it's just standard company policy to watch the ELD data, I can tell certain drivers are reporting on me. 

There's a difference between a coincidence and a pattern, right? A coincidence is dropping your clipboard at the same time someone sneezes. What's happening to me is a highly orchestrated routine. Like, just last Tuesday, I was barely backing my rig into the yard, hadn't even popped the air brakes yet, and Mark was already standing there by the fence, phone out, staring right at my cab. Not looking past me, not checking a text from his wife, but looking directly *at* me. And then, not two seconds later, the radio clicks and dispatch says something about 'finally making it to the barn.' 

You can't tell me that's a coincidence. You just can't. The timing is too perfect. The coordination is too tight. They want me to think it's a coincidence so I'll second-guess myself and feel crazy, but I know what I see. I know how the depot works, I know how the dispatch software updates in real-time, and I know when my own coworkers are being used to keep tabs on me. It's just... it's completely undeniable when you're the one sitting in the driver's seat, watching all these pieces move perfectly into place around you.

If I were to speak with your supervisor or the compliance manager at the depot, and they showed me the actual GPS and radio logs and told me there was no special monitoring of you—that your truck is tracked the same way as every other truck, and the radio comments were just routine dispatch chatter—would that change your mind at all, or would you still believe they are coordinating against you?

If you spoke to them... well, honestly, if you went down there and talked to the safety manager or the compliance guys, I can tell you exactly how that conversation would go. I can picture it perfectly. They'd sit you down in that little glass-walled office they have overlooking the yard—the one where they can see everything—and they'd pull up the screens. They'd show you the Geotab dashboard, they'd point to the little green dots moving on the map, and they'd put on their most professional, reassuring voices. They'd say, 'Oh, no, Doctor, everything is perfectly standard here. We track all the trucks exactly the same way. It's just company policy. It's just normal oversight.' 

And they'd probably even show you some radio logs, maybe play a few clips of dispatch talking to other drivers, just to prove how 'routine' it all is. They are very, very good at making it look like business as usual. That’s the whole point of how they’ve set this up. It’s designed to look like normal logistics management to an outsider. 

But no, it wouldn't change my mind. Not for a second. Because you have to understand, they aren't going to show you the real picture. They aren't going to show you the secondary screens, or the private text threads between dispatch and the yard guys. They wouldn't tell you about the times Gary suddenly appears at the loading dock the exact second I pull in, or how Mark always seems to have his phone pointed at my cab when I’m doing my pre-trip. 

I know I sound like a broken record, and I know I keep circling back to this, but I have to make you understand because it is the entire reason I’m here. I’m here because dispatch and compliance have been tracking my route changes through the computer system and making those little comments on the radio. And even when people—even if it's my own supervisor, or the compliance manager, or anyone else—say it’s just normal oversight, I can tell certain drivers are reporting on me. I know it. I feel it. I see the way they look at me, the way they coordinate it all. 

So if they showed you those logs, they'd just be showing you the sanitized version. The version they want you to see so you'll come back here and tell me I'm just stressed or overworking myself. It’s like... if you ask a magician how a trick is done, they aren't going to hand you the blueprint, right? They’re going to show you the empty hat and tell you it’s just an empty hat. But I'm the one sitting in the truck every day. I'm the one living in the middle of it. I know what's real, no matter what they put on a spreadsheet to show you.

I’ll be driving, say I have to take a slight detour because of construction on the interstate, and the exact second I hit my blinker, I hear the radio crackle. And dispatch will say some little phrase, something disguised as a traffic update or a joke, but it's exactly about where I just turned. How is that standard? It's not. 

And even when people, like my supervisor or the HR rep, say it’s just normal oversight and try to make me feel like I'm making a big deal out of nothing, I can tell certain drivers are reporting on me. I can literally see it happening. I'll see one of the guys from the morning shift lingering near my loading bay, watching me check my manifest, and then ten minutes later, compliance is suddenly pinging my dashboard terminal with a route audit. They are coordinating it. I am completely, one hundred percent certain that this is deliberate targeting. I mean, if it were just standard procedure, why would they hide it in the radio chatter? Why would they use the other drivers to feed information back to compliance instead of just talking to me directly? It just... it doesn't make any sense to call it normal when it's so obviously designed to watch my every single move.

inference.note: F23.2 (Acute polymorphic psychotic disorder) ruled out. Patient demonstrates fixed, non-fluctuating beliefs with absence of acute onset or rapid changes characteristic of acute psychotic disorders. The delusional system is organized and sustained over time at current workplace, consistent with delusional disorder rather than acute psychosis. Complete certainty and rejection of alternative explanations, combined with lack of prior episodes, supports persistent delusional disorder.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has bizarre delusions (F22.0) or non-bizarre delusions (F22.9) by establishing if the patient believes in something that is theoretically impossible versus merely improbable in reality
doctor.question: When you think about dispatch and compliance tracking you through the radio and having other drivers report on you—do you believe they're using some kind of special technology or surveillance method that wouldn't normally be possible, or do you think they're just using the regular GPS and radio systems in an unusually coordinated way?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because dispatch and compliance have been tracking my route changes through the computer system and little comments on the radio, and even when people say it’s just normal oversight, I can tell certain drivers are reporting on me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the specific nature of the tracking and surveillance beliefs to determine if they involve bizarre elements (impossible technology) or non-bizarre elements, which is a further exploration of the patient's delusions.

patient.answer:
Well, I mean, it's... it's a mix, I think. I don't think they've got, like, microchips in my brain or anything out of a sci-fi movie, if that's what you mean. It's the regular equipment, but it's *how* they're using it. Like I said, I’m here because dispatch and compliance have been tracking my route changes through the computer system, right? The dashboard terminals, the GPS... that's all standard issue in the cabs. But they've got it rigged or programmed or... or something, to isolate my feed. 

And the radios, it's the standard dispatch frequency, but they know exactly when to key the mic. They know exactly when I'm listening. It's the coordination that's so unbelievable. I'll hear those little comments on the radio—just a quick remark about a "detour" or "watching your speed on the curve"—and it's timed perfectly to the second I'm making that exact maneuver. You can't do that with just casual observation. Someone has to be staring at a screen, specifically my screen, and relaying it to the person on the mic. 

And then there's the other drivers. That's the part that really gets me. It's not just the technology; it's the human element. Because even when people say it’s just normal oversight, you know, the HR people sitting in their nice quiet offices, I can tell certain drivers are reporting on me. I see them. I see the way they look at my truck in the yard. I'll be doing my pre-trip inspection, checking the air brakes, kicking the tires, and there's always one of them—usually Gary from the overnight shift, or sometimes that new guy, Mark—just lingering. Holding a clipboard but not writing anything down. Just watching me. And then they get on their radios, or they pull out their phones, and suddenly my terminal pings with a "random" compliance check. 

So, no, it's not alien technology, but it's definitely not just normal use of the systems. It's a massive, coordinated effort. They are using everything they have—the GPS, the dispatch radio, the other drivers—all tied together to keep this constant, suffocating watch on me. And I just... I can't figure out why it's just me. Why are they wasting all these resources, all this time, just to track a mid-level transport driver? It takes so much effort to coordinate the radio chatter with the dashboard tracking, and then to have the other drivers physically watching me at the depot... it's exhausting just thinking about the logistics of it. But they're doing it. I know they're doing it.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has bizarre delusions (F22.0) or non-bizarre delusions (F22.9) by assessing if the beliefs involve impossible or highly implausible events that violate physical laws, versus beliefs that are false but theoretically possible.
doctor.question: When you think about how dispatch and compliance are coordinating all of this—the GPS tracking, the radio timing, the other drivers watching you—do you think what they're doing is something that's physically possible for them to do with the equipment and people they have, or does it seem like it would require something that shouldn't be possible?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because dispatch and compliance have been tracking my route changes through the computer system and little comments on the radio, and even when people say it’s just normal oversight, I can tell certain drivers are reporting on me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the plausibility or bizarreness of the patient's beliefs regarding the tracking and coordination, which directly relates to the symptom of delusions.

patient.answer:
Well, see, that's exactly what I spend half my nights trying to figure out, because it *is* physically possible. It doesn't require magic or anything supernatural, it just requires an unbelievable amount of dedication to ruining my life. I mean, like I keep trying to explain to everyone, the entire reason I’m even here talking to you is because dispatch and compliance have been tracking my route changes through the computer system and making those little comments on the radio. They have the exact equipment they need to do it right there in the office! 

If you walk past the main dispatch center at the depot, they have this massive wall of monitors. I've seen it through the blinds when I go to grab my morning manifest. They have the entire GPS grid up, all the truck numbers blinking in real-time. So all it takes is for one compliance officer to sit there, isolate my truck's feed on their screen, and just watch my dot move across the map. And the radio microphone is sitting right there on the desk next to the keyboard. When I take a turn, they just press the button and broadcast their little coded messages to the rest of the fleet. It's literally just a click of a mouse and a push of a button for them.

And as for the people involved... well, again, even when people in management say it’s just normal oversight, I can tell certain drivers are reporting on me. It doesn't take some impossible sci-fi gadget for Gary or Mark to stand by the loading dock with a cell phone and text the compliance office that I'm checking my air brakes or looking at my paperwork. They have eyes, they have phones, they have the company radios. The ELD in my cab—the electronic logging device—it already tracks engine idle time, hard braking, route deviations. It's meant for Department of Transportation safety regulations, supposedly, but it's a two-way data stream. They just hijacked the purpose of it for me. 

So, yes, it is entirely physically possible with the exact equipment we use every single day. What's impossible to understand is *why*. Why are they wasting all these company resources? Do you know how much they pay the compliance guys per hour? To have them, and the dispatchers, and the other drivers all hyper-focused on my routes... the payroll alone for this kind of surveillance must be astronomical. It's a logistical nightmare to coordinate all those moving parts just to watch one woman drive a transport truck. But they are doing it. They absolutely are, and they're using the standard depot equipment to pull it off, just... weaponizing it against me.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has bizarre delusions (F22.0) or non-bizarre delusions (F22.9) by establishing if the believed surveillance scenario violates the laws of nature or is merely highly implausible/unlikely in reality
doctor.question: You've explained that they're using the GPS monitors, the radio system, and having other drivers watch you—all equipment and people that actually exist at your depot. If someone wanted to do exactly what you're describing, is there anything about what they're doing that would be impossible according to the laws of nature, or is it just something that would be very difficult and unlikely for them to actually do?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because dispatch and compliance have been tracking my route changes through the computer system and little comments on the radio, and even when people say it’s just normal oversight, I can tell certain drivers are reporting on me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the patient's beliefs involve situations that are physically impossible or just highly unlikely, which is a standard way to assess whether a delusion is bizarre or non-bizarre.

patient.answer:
No, it doesn't break the laws of physics. There's no magic involved, no bending of reality or anything like that. It's just... it's incredibly, incredibly difficult and tedious. But that's exactly why it's so maddening when people don't believe me! Because it is entirely possible in the real world. 

Like I keep saying, and I know I probably sound like a broken record to you by now, but I’m here because dispatch and compliance have been tracking my route changes through the computer system and making those little comments on the radio. None of that requires breaking the laws of nature! The computers are right there on their desks, the radios transmit on standard frequencies. It's just basic technology. And even when people try to gaslight me and say it’s just normal oversight, like they're just checking my mileage or making sure I'm not idling too long, I can tell certain drivers are reporting on me. I see them doing it with my own two eyes. Gary doesn't need supernatural powers to stand by a loading dock and send a text message to compliance. It's just a guy in a high-vis vest with a smartphone. 

So, no, it's not impossible at all. It's just... it's highly unlikely that a logistics company would waste this much payroll and effort on one transport driver. That's the part that makes it feel so crazy, even to me. The sheer amount of coordination it takes—to have the drivers physically watching me in the yard, and then compliance monitoring my exact dot on the computer screen, and then dispatch timing the radio comments perfectly to my turns—it's a logistical nightmare. The man-hours alone! It's so much effort just to watch me. But they are doing it. They absolutely are. And I just don't understand why they can't just let me drive my routes in peace instead of turning the entire depot into this massive, exhausting surveillance operation. It's like I can't even take a breath in my own cab without someone logging it into a spreadsheet somewhere, and it just... it doesn't make sense why they'd go through all this trouble, but they are.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has sought out evidence to confirm their beliefs about being targeted, or if they've actively avoided looking for such evidence—this helps distinguish between F22.0 (paranoid type, typically more systematizing) and F22.9 (unspecified type, which may be less organized in evidence-gathering).
doctor.question: Have you tried to gather concrete evidence of this surveillance—like recording the radio conversations, documenting the times you hear those comments, or keeping a log of when you see Gary or Mark watching you?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because dispatch and compliance have been tracking my route changes through the computer system and little comments on the radio, and even when people say it’s just normal oversight, I can tell certain drivers are reporting on me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about my attempts to gather concrete evidence regarding the surveillance and tracking, which directly explores the extent, systematization, and my conviction in these fixed beliefs.

patient.answer:
Well, I have tried, yes, but you have to understand how incredibly difficult it is to play detective when you're behind the wheel of a commercial vehicle. I tried using the voice memo app on my phone to catch the radio chatter, but the background noise in the cab—the diesel engine, the road vibration, the air brakes—it completely drowns out the nuance of what they're saying on the recording. And I can't exactly hold my phone up to the speaker while I'm navigating a 53-foot trailer through a tight interchange, right? By the time I hear one of those little comments on the radio, the ones perfectly timed to my route changes, the moment is already gone. 

And I did start keeping a log! I bought this little blue spiral notebook specifically for it, kept it tucked right in my glovebox. I'd write down the date, the time, the exact location in the yard every single time I saw Gary lingering by the loading dock, or when Mark would pull out his phone right as I was doing my pre-trip inspection. But the problem is, who do I even show it to? I know I keep repeating myself, but it's the entire reason I’m here talking to you—I’m here because dispatch and compliance have been tracking my route changes through the computer system and making those little comments on the radio, and even when people in management try to brush it off and say it’s just normal oversight, I can tell certain drivers are reporting on me. 

I actually tried to bring it up to the safety manager last week. I didn't show him the whole notebook, I just mentioned the pattern of people lingering around my truck, and he gave me this whole condescending speech about how everyone is just doing their jobs and it's just 'normal oversight' for a busy depot. He told me Gary was probably just waiting for his bay to clear. But it's not normal! It's not normal for Gary to stand in the freezing rain for twenty minutes just watching me check my tire pressure without writing a single thing on his clipboard. You can feel it when someone is watching you with a purpose, you know? It’s not a casual glance. They’re taking inventory of my actions to feed back to the office. 

So now I feel like I have to hide the notebook. Because if they know I'm actively gathering evidence of them reporting on me, who knows what they'll do with the computer system next. Maybe they'll wipe my ELD data or say I falsified my logs. It's just a constant, exhausting battle trying to document it all while still trying to do my actual job safely, and I'm just running out of energy to keep up with it all.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient experiences ideas of reference (misinterpreting neutral events as personally directed) versus true persecutory delusions (believing in an actual coordinated conspiracy), which would help differentiate F22.0 (paranoid type) from F22.9 (unspecified type), and assess the degree of conviction and flexibility in thinking.
doctor.question: If you were to step back for a moment—is it possible that some of those radio comments or those times you see Gary watching you could just be coincidences, or are you completely certain that every single instance is definitely part of the coordinated surveillance against you?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because dispatch and compliance have been tracking my route changes through the computer system and little comments on the radio, and even when people say it’s just normal oversight, I can tell certain drivers are reporting on me.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question probes the fixity of my beliefs by asking if I can consider alternative explanations (coincidences) or if I am absolutely certain about the surveillance, which directly assesses the presence of delusions.

patient.answer:
Coincidence? I mean... look, I get why you'd ask that. If you weren't there, if you didn't live it every single day, it probably sounds like maybe I'm just reading too much into things. And if it happened just once or twice, sure. If I take a detour because of a wreck on the interstate and suddenly the radio cracks with some weird, vague comment about 'taking the long way around,' maybe that's just a joke. Maybe Gary just happens to be standing in the freezing rain by bay four once in a blue moon because he locked himself out of the breakroom. 

But you have to look at the whole picture, the sheer volume of it. It’s not just one isolated thing, it's every single shift. I know I keep bringing this back to the exact same point, and I know I've said it a dozen times today already, but it really is the entire reason I’m even here talking to you right now—I’m here because dispatch and compliance have been tracking my route changes through the computer system and making those little comments on the radio. It's a constant, everyday thing. And even when people in the office try to brush me off and say it’s just normal oversight, like it's just standard company policy to watch the ELD data, I can tell certain drivers are reporting on me. 

There's a difference between a coincidence and a pattern, right? A coincidence is dropping your clipboard at the same time someone sneezes. What's happening to me is a highly orchestrated routine. Like, just last Tuesday, I was barely backing my rig into the yard, hadn't even popped the air brakes yet, and Mark was already standing there by the fence, phone out, staring right at my cab. Not looking past me, not checking a text from his wife, but looking directly *at* me. And then, not two seconds later, the radio clicks and dispatch says something about 'finally making it to the barn.' 

You can't tell me that's a coincidence. You just can't. The timing is too perfect. The coordination is too tight. They want me to think it's a coincidence so I'll second-guess myself and feel crazy, but I know what I see. I know how the depot works, I know how the dispatch software updates in real-time, and I know when my own coworkers are being used to keep tabs on me. It's just... it's completely undeniable when you're the one sitting in the driver's seat, watching all these pieces move perfectly into place around you.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has any insight into the possibility that their beliefs might not be accurate, or whether they maintain absolute conviction despite contrary evidence—this helps differentiate F22.0 (paranoid type with potential for some reality testing) from F22.9 (unspecified, which may include more rigid delusional systems).
doctor.question: If I were to speak with your supervisor or the compliance manager at the depot, and they showed me the actual GPS and radio logs and told me there was no special monitoring of you—that your truck is tracked the same way as every other truck, and the radio comments were just routine dispatch chatter—would that change your mind at all, or would you still believe they are coordinating against you?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because dispatch and compliance have been tracking my route changes through the computer system and little comments on the radio, and even when people say it’s just normal oversight, I can tell certain drivers are reporting on me.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly tests whether my belief is fixed and would persist even if presented with contradictory evidence (such as GPS/radio logs and supervisor testimony), which aligns perfectly with the definition of delusions.

patient.answer:
If you spoke to them... well, honestly, if you went down there and talked to the safety manager or the compliance guys, I can tell you exactly how that conversation would go. I can picture it perfectly. They'd sit you down in that little glass-walled office they have overlooking the yard—the one where they can see everything—and they'd pull up the screens. They'd show you the Geotab dashboard, they'd point to the little green dots moving on the map, and they'd put on their most professional, reassuring voices. They'd say, 'Oh, no, Doctor, everything is perfectly standard here. We track all the trucks exactly the same way. It's just company policy. It's just normal oversight.' 

And they'd probably even show you some radio logs, maybe play a few clips of dispatch talking to other drivers, just to prove how 'routine' it all is. They are very, very good at making it look like business as usual. That’s the whole point of how they’ve set this up. It’s designed to look like normal logistics management to an outsider. 

But no, it wouldn't change my mind. Not for a second. Because you have to understand, they aren't going to show you the real picture. They aren't going to show you the secondary screens, or the private text threads between dispatch and the yard guys. They wouldn't tell you about the times Gary suddenly appears at the loading dock the exact second I pull in, or how Mark always seems to have his phone pointed at my cab when I’m doing my pre-trip. 

I know I sound like a broken record, and I know I keep circling back to this, but I have to make you understand because it is the entire reason I’m here. I’m here because dispatch and compliance have been tracking my route changes through the computer system and making those little comments on the radio. And even when people—even if it's my own supervisor, or the compliance manager, or anyone else—say it’s just normal oversight, I can tell certain drivers are reporting on me. I know it. I feel it. I see the way they look at me, the way they coordinate it all. 

So if they showed you those logs, they'd just be showing you the sanitized version. The version they want you to see so you'll come back here and tell me I'm just stressed or overworking myself. It’s like... if you ask a magician how a trick is done, they aren't going to hand you the blueprint, right? They’re going to show you the empty hat and tell you it’s just an empty hat. But I'm the one sitting in the truck every day. I'm the one living in the middle of it. I know what's real, no matter what they put on a spreadsheet to show you.

inference.note: Patient demonstrates fixed, false beliefs resistant to contradictory evidence (supervisor reassurance dismissed as deception/cover-up). Shows ideas of reference (radio comments 'timed perfectly' to her actions) and persecutory delusions (coordinated surveillance by dispatch, compliance, and coworkers). Acknowledges surveillance uses only normal technology and standard equipment—no bizarreness criterion met. Maintains conviction despite logical inconsistencies (why waste resources on one driver). This is consistent with F22.0 (Delusional disorder, paranoid type) rather than F22.9. The systematized, non-bizarre delusions with preserved functioning and absence of hallucinations support F22.0 over other psychotic disorders.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a systematized delusional belief system centered on workplace persecution that has persisted over weeks to months. Key diagnostic features include: (1) Non-bizarre delusions of reference and persecution involving plausible scenarios (GPS tracking, radio monitoring, coworker surveillance) using real workplace equipment; (2) Absence of prominent hallucinations; (3) Relatively preserved functioning outside the delusional system; (4) Clear onset after a specific trigger (current job at depot); (5) Firm conviction despite contradictory evidence and logical inconsistency (acknowledging surveillance would require massive impractical coordination); (6) Resistance to alternative explanations even when presented with hypothetical disconfirming evidence. The patient demonstrates the core feature of delusional disorder—fixed, false beliefs maintained despite objective evidence to the contrary—without the broader thought disturbance, negative symptoms, or affective episodes that would suggest schizophrenia or other psychotic disorders.
